note: One height for every mastaba in the OSM footprint import, which traces outlines and tags no heights. Four metres is a massing figure so the cemetery fields read as a field of low solid tombs rather than as outlines on the sand: the Giza mastabas were built to several times that, and most now stand far lower, so the sigma is half the value and nothing should be concluded from any one of them. Replace it with a per-tomb height from Reisner or the Giza Archives when one is to hand. Checked against Reisner on 2026-09-16 (source reisner-1942): the core mastabas of cemetery G 1200 in his Appendix A stand to a maximum height of 5.1 m (p. 389), 4.1 m (p. 392), c. 5.0 m (p. 394) and 5.0 m (p. 396), and the other tombs whose height the text layer gives cleanly run from 3 to 6 m. Their areas cluster so closely (254 to 262 sq. m) that no height can be scaled from an outline's size, so the one figure stands, and it errs low for a core mastaba as built.

One height for the six temples in the OSM footprint import: the mortuary and valley temples of Khafre and Menkaure, the Sphinx Temple and the temple of Amenhotep II. They survive very unequally, Khafre's valley temple standing to its roof in places and Menkaure's mortuary temple barely above its foundations, so this is a massing figure with a wide sigma, not a claim about any of them.

Khafre's satellite pyramid, G2-a, south of his pyramid, survives as little more than its foundation. OSM traces the footprint and gives no height; three metres keeps it visible as a ruin and says nothing about what it was.

The Wall of the Crow, the great limestone wall at the south-east of the plateau between the pyramids and the workers' town. OSM traces a short stretch and tags no height; eight metres is a massing figure for a wall that stands to roughly that order, with a sigma to say it is not measured.

How far each boat pit in the OSM footprint import is cut below the ground it is traced on. The pits east of the Great Pyramid are deep rock-cut trenches and OSM gives only their outlines, so six metres is a figure chosen to draw them as cuts rather than as marks on the surface.

The mean of the "general batter" Reisner gives for the stepped retaining walls of core mastabas in the Western Field, Appendix A: 74°27′ (p. 385), 74°57′ (p. 389), 74°3′ (p. 392), 74°18′ (p. 394), 75°36′ (p. 396), 74°45′ (p. 398), 74°30′ (p. 408), 73°37′ (p. 412) and 77°19′ (p. 418), measured "by a line touching the edges of the steps" from the horizontal. Two more on pp. 403 and 407 come through the text layer garbled ("7.2 degrees 52 minutes", "7.4 degrees and 18 minutes") and are left out. Sigma is the spread of the nine. These are one cemetery's core mastabas, stepped courses about 37 cm high set back about 10 cm; every mastaba outline OSM traces is drawn with this batter, which is a plausible form for the field and not a survey of any one tomb.

The mean of the average height of the stepped courses Reisner gives for the same nine core mastabas of the Western Field as tier3.mastaba.batter, Appendix A: 37.2 cm (p. 385), 36.6 (p. 389), 34.2 (p. 392), 37.2 (p. 394), 38 (p. 396), 26.1 (p. 398), 38.7 (p. 408), 35.6 (p. 412) and 31.1 (p. 418). Sigma is their spread. The renders band the mastaba field's stone at this period; nothing is built from it.
